item.title: The Human and the Swarm
item.description:
In the article "AI and the Inflation of Quality," I wrote that the sharp decrease in the cost of intellectual labor is rapidly changing our requirements for its results. If an additional check takes a few minutes, people start doing it. If ten options can be quickly reviewed, the first one that comes to mind no longer seems sufficient. Yesterday's "too long and expensive" becomes today's "why not?", and quality begins to grow along with capabilities. This process has another aspect that is somewhat lost in the endless comparison of humans and machines. We are used to counting AI individually. Can one agent write code better than one programmer? How much more productive is one analyst with AI than an analyst without it? How many employees can a person with a good electronic assistant replace? These are reasonable questions that lead to equally reasonable labor market arithmetic: if one employee now does the work of two, the second becomes redundant. A Division of Mathematicians But then OpenAI demonstrated a different way of counting intelligence. To work on the Navier-Stokes problem, they launched about 10,000 agents that worked for 88 hours. And what's more interesting to me in this story is not another round of discussion about how smart the models have become, but the number itself. Ten thousand. If you put ten thousand good live mathematicians on one problem for 88 hours, I would also expect something interesting from them. The question is how exactly to put them to work. Ten thousand mathematicians need to be divided into groups, directions assigned, intermediate results collected, duplication noticed, dead-end branches closed, useful findings transferred between groups, and people constantly reassigned to where progress is being made. After some time, the mathematical problem begins to compete for attention with the problem of managing a division of mathematicians. Read more

item.title: Jumping into Infinity: How RBF SVM Works Under the Hood
item.description:
Hello everyone! My name is Andrey, I am a 4th-year student at the Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, and the author of the Telegram channel Andre | Data Science. We all know that machine learning is currently on a huge hype - almost from under every stone, they talk about various methods and how they can solve almost any problem. But there are catastrophically few guides that would thoroughly analyze the work of a specific method - from ordinary data loading to mathematical justification of its working principle and visualization of each step. In this article, I want to fill this gap and analyze one specific method - RBF SVM. We will look at how it is structured from a mathematical point of view, how it came to be, what its strengths and weaknesses are, and what they are related to. We will also test it on real datasets. Since the audience of the IT community is quite broad, I will try to describe each definition and each part of my narrative in great detail, so that as you read, you have as few questions as possible and the thread of understanding does not break. It will be a big plus if you are already familiar with the following mathematical disciplines: Linear algebra, Mathematical analysis, Functional analysis, Differential equations, Optimization methods, Analytical geometry.

item.title: MoVA: a new attention architecture
item.description:
About the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, everyone who follows ML has heard: Mixtral and DeepSeek have proven the effectiveness of dynamic routing. But while the industry is mastering basic MoE, its direct successor called MoVA has emerged. In this article, we will break down: how classic MoE works, what exactly MoVA changes in the attention mechanism, how it architecturally differs from MoE, and how it all looks in a specific model, with numbers, benchmarks, and the first independent reviews. Read more

item.title: GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning — the first Russian open model with reasoning capabilities
item.description:
Hello, Habr. We are releasing GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning, the first GigaChat model with full reasoning capabilities, trained using online RL technology. The main change in training: after SFT, the model underwent online RL entirely. Not just one domain or one final stage, but six separate experts (mathematics, code, agents, and others), each with its own reward, which were then combined back into a single model. In this article, we will discuss not only the numbers but also how the pipeline is structured, how the model exploited rewards, and why all this took over nine months. Read more

item.title: 350 commits a week: how to contribute to a project that changes faster than you can write
item.description:
Imagine: a night alert, the application is returning 500s, but it's alive. It's clear that the familiar process will begin – tabs with graphs, searches in logs, and attempts to understand who changed what. How much time does this usually take? What if an AI agent helps you investigate the incident? Hi! I'm Anton Vorontsov, CRE at Yandex Cloud. At the end of July, I was browsing fresh GitHub repositories again to see what's happening in my related disciplines: SRE, automation, and, of course, AI. Suddenly, I stumbled upon an interesting repository that was actively growing: the number of stars, commits, and interested people from different countries – all about OpenSRE. This article is about my first contribution to an external project, what was the most challenging part, and how this tool works. Read more

item.title: AI Agents in Production: Sandboxing, RBAC, and Egress Gateways Instead of Relying on Prompts
item.description:
According to Gartner, task-specific AI agents will be embedded in 40% of enterprise applications by the end of 2026. Security is often limited to guardrails and prompt filters. However, incidents like Replit deleting a production database and user data leakage via Claude highlight the need for robust security. CNCF's recent materials suggest a multi-layered approach involving sandboxing, RBAC, and egress control. This article explores how to build a secure operational environment for AI agents using these principles, focusing on Kubernetes-native solutions.

item.title: How I Remastered "Tom and Jerry" in 4K Over Two Years: Take Two
item.description:
Two years ago, I released my debut guide on remastering classic "Tom and Jerry" in 2K. The article garnered hundreds of thousands of views and hundreds of upvotes, but I was rightly criticized by professionals in the comments. The picture stopped flickering and being covered in scratches, but in return, I got the "uncanny valley" effect and tons of AI-generated soapiness. I decided my favorite childhood cartoon deserved better. Over two years, I made five attempts; I painstakingly developed working tools only to discard thousands of hours of completed work. A new start, and finally, the final attempt. Meow meow

item.title: Why an AI Agent When You Have Dashboards? Answering Questions About Live 1C Data
item.description:
Imagine a common work situation. In an approval task, you need to quickly understand if a specific payment has gone through. Not 'what was the total volume of payments this month,' but specifically: has the money for this invoice arrived, what was the amount, when was it recorded in 1C, and is there a discrepancy with what's indicated in the workflow? A dashboard might not have this answer. It displays pre-selected metrics, and no one will design, approve, and maintain a new widget for a single check. You could open 1C, find the document, verify the details, and then return to your workspace. If such questions arise infrequently, this path seems tolerable—until these infrequent questions become numerous. It's precisely for these situations that we've added an AI agent to the workflow workspace, capable of accessing current 1C data and answering questions within the task's context. The agent operates in read-only mode under a separate 1C account with limited privileges and indicates the actual data it relied upon. In this article, we'll explain why the agent doesn't replace dashboards, which tasks are best suited for each tool, and what's needed to ensure AI model answers about corporate data are verifiable. Read on.

item.title: AI Industry Has Voluntarily Put Itself in Handcuffs. Let's See If They're Real
item.description:
On September 1st, OpenAI published a document titled "Path to Astra: critical capabilities and frontier safeguards." I opened it casually, over tea, with about the same interest as one reads terms of service updates. Forty minutes later, my tea had gone cold, and I was sitting with the company's August publications open in adjacent tabs, trying to figure out when exactly everything had managed to change. Formally, the document states the following: Astra, OpenAI's next major model, has been recognized as reaching the Critical level for cybersecurity within the company's internal risk assessment system. It's the first model in OpenAI's history with such a classification. The release is delayed, and security measures are enhanced. And one more line, which was mentioned least often in the news: Astra became the first model to undergo formal pre-release cybersecurity review by the US government. It's this line that got me stuck. Because no one forced them to do it. And no one forced the company to call for it. Two days later, the model was released. OpenAI President Greg Brockman closed the briefing with the words "Welcome to the AGI era," and almost all the press focused on that. Almost no one wrote about the pre-release review. Read more

item.title: Where Claude Code Actually Goes: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, Two Key Types, and /status
item.description:
Claude Code isn't tied to api.anthropic.com: it's a regular client, and where it sends requests is determined by two variables. I'll break down what it needs from the endpoint, three connection methods (shell, settings.json, apiKeyHelper), how to check with curl before launching, and what common errors mean—401, 403 with HTML, 'auth may not work as expected,' and a sudden 404 on haiku. No service names, just mechanics. Read more
